title: Regex: Patterns and Syntax

sources.name: Original explanations and examples from general programming knowledge
MDN: selected JavaScript character escape checks
MDN: selected Unicode property escape checks

description: For developers practicing regex syntax, matching, groups, assertions, and common pitfalls. Examples use JavaScript unless stated otherwise; engine differences are identified explicitly.

cards.front: What does a literal regex character match?
cards.back: It normally matches itself unless it has a special syntactic role.
cards.example: The pattern cat finds cat within concatenate.

cards.front: What does . match in JavaScript without the s flag?
cards.back: Any one character except a line terminator; Unicode mode affects how characters are counted.
cards.example: a.c matches abc but not a followed by a newline and c.

cards.front: What does \. match?
cards.back: A literal period rather than the wildcard dot.
cards.example: a\.b matches a.b.

cards.front: What does \\ match in regex source?
cards.back: A literal backslash. Host-language strings may require additional escaping.
cards.example: The regex source \\ finds the backslash in a path.

cards.front: What does [abc] match?
cards.back: One character chosen from a, b, or c.
cards.example: [abc] finds b in dogbed.

cards.front: What does [^abc] match?
cards.back: One character other than a, b, or c.
cards.example: [^abc] finds d in abcd.

cards.front: What does [a-z] match without special flags?
cards.back: One ASCII lowercase letter from a through z.
cards.example: [a-z]+ finds sun in 7sun8.

cards.front: What does [A-Z] match without the i flag?
cards.back: One ASCII uppercase letter from A through Z.
cards.example: [A-Z]+ finds NASA in NASA2026.

cards.front: What does [0-9] match?
cards.back: One ASCII digit.
cards.example: [0-9]+ finds 204 in room204.

cards.front: How can a basic character class include a literal hyphen?
cards.back: Place it first or last in the class, or escape it where the chosen mode permits.
cards.example: [-a] matches either a hyphen or a.

cards.front: What does \d match in JavaScript?
cards.back: An ASCII digit, equivalent to [0-9].
cards.example: \d+ finds 52 in item52.

cards.front: What does uppercase \D match in JavaScript?
cards.back: One character that is not an ASCII digit.
cards.example: \D+ finds abc in 123abc.

cards.front: What does \w match in ordinary JavaScript regex use?
cards.back: ASCII letters, ASCII digits, and underscore; Unicode-aware case folding with the i flag can add limited equivalents. It is not a general all-language word class.
cards.example: \w+ matches user_7.

cards.front: What does \W match?
cards.back: A character not matched by \w under the same engine and flags.
cards.example: \W finds the hyphen in user-name.

cards.front: What does \s match in JavaScript?
cards.back: One whitespace or line-terminator character from JavaScript's defined set.
cards.example: \s+ can match spaces, tabs, and newlines.

cards.front: What does \S match?
cards.back: One character that is not matched by \s.
cards.example: \S+ finds red in a string beginning with spaces followed by red.

cards.front: What does \t match?
cards.back: A horizontal tab character.
cards.example: a\tb matches a and b separated by a tab.

cards.front: What does \n match?
cards.back: A line-feed character.
cards.example: The pattern \n finds a Unix-style line break.

cards.front: What does \r match?
cards.back: A carriage-return character.
cards.example: \r\n matches a common Windows line-ending sequence.

cards.front: What does \b assert outside a character class?
cards.back: A boundary between a word character and a nonword character, or an appropriate string edge; the definition of word character is engine-dependent.
cards.example: \bcat\b matches cat in a cat sleeps.

cards.front: What does \B assert?
cards.back: A position that is not a word boundary.
cards.example: \Bcat finds cat inside concatenate.

cards.front: What does ^ assert in JavaScript without m?
cards.back: The beginning of the input.
cards.example: ^cat matches catnap but not bobcat.

cards.front: What does $ assert in JavaScript without m?
cards.back: The end of the input. Other engines may also allow a position before a final newline.
cards.example: cat$ matches bobcat but not catnap.

cards.front: What does the m flag change in JavaScript?
cards.back: It lets ^ and $ also match appropriate line boundaries within the input.
cards.example: /^cat/m can match cat at the start of a later line.

cards.front: What does the i flag request?
cards.back: Case-insensitive matching according to the engine's case-folding rules.
cards.example: /cat/i matches Cat.

cards.front: What does the s flag change?
cards.back: It lets the wildcard dot match line terminators as well.
cards.example: /a.b/s matches a, a newline, then b.

cards.front: What does the g flag do in JavaScript?
cards.back: It enables global matching behavior in relevant APIs and makes exec and test use and update lastIndex. Zero-length matches require care when iterating.
cards.example: A global match for /a/g can find all three a characters in banana.

cards.front: What does the u flag enable in JavaScript?
cards.back: Unicode-aware parsing and matching, including code-point escapes and Unicode property escapes.
cards.example: /\u{1F600}/u represents one specified Unicode code point.

cards.front: What does x* mean?
cards.back: Zero or more repetitions of x, greedily by default.
cards.example: ab*c matches ac, abc, and abbbc.

cards.front: What does x+ mean?
cards.back: One or more repetitions of x, greedily by default.
cards.example: ab+c matches abc but not ac.

cards.front: What does x? mean as a quantifier?
cards.back: Zero or one occurrence of x.
cards.example: colou?r matches color and colour.

cards.front: What does x{3} mean?
cards.back: Exactly three repetitions of x.
cards.example: a{3} matches aaa.

cards.front: What does x{2,4} mean?
cards.back: Between two and four repetitions of x, inclusive.
cards.example: a{2,4} can match aa, aaa, or aaaa.

cards.front: What does x{2,} mean?
cards.back: At least two repetitions of x.
cards.example: a{2,} matches a run of two or more a characters.

cards.front: What is a greedy quantifier?
cards.back: A quantifier that initially prefers as many repetitions as possible while still allowing the overall match to succeed.
cards.example: On a12b34b, a.*b matches the whole string.

cards.front: What is a lazy quantifier?
cards.back: A quantifier followed by ? that initially prefers fewer repetitions while still allowing a match.
cards.example: On a12b34b, a.*?b first matches a12b.

cards.front: How do you make + lazy?
cards.back: Use +?.
cards.example: a+? initially matches one a within aaaa.

cards.front: How do you make {2,5} lazy?
cards.example: a{2,5}? initially matches two a characters in aaaaa.

cards.front: What does a quantifier apply to?
cards.back: The immediately preceding atom or group, not automatically to the whole preceding expression.
cards.example: ab+ repeats b; (ab)+ repeats the pair ab.

cards.front: What does cat|dog mean?
cards.back: Match either the cat alternative or the dog alternative.
cards.example: The pattern can find dog in a dog runs.

cards.front: Why group alternatives when adding anchors?
cards.back: Alternation has low precedence; grouping makes the anchors apply to all branches.
cards.example: ^(?:cat|dog)$ accepts the whole string cat or dog.

cards.front: What does (abc) create?
cards.back: A capturing group that groups tokens and stores the matched text.
cards.example: (ab)+ captures the final ab iteration in JavaScript.

cards.front: What does (?:abc) create?
cards.back: A noncapturing group that groups tokens without creating a numbered capture.
cards.example: (?:ab)+ matches repeated ab units.

cards.front: How are ordinary capturing groups numbered?
cards.back: By the position of their opening parentheses, starting at 1; noncapturing groups do not get a number.
cards.example: In (a)(?:b)(c), c is group 2.

cards.front: What does \1 mean after a first capturing group exists?
cards.back: A backreference to the text captured by group 1.
cards.example: ([a-z])\1 matches oo in book.

cards.front: How can a backreference require matching quote characters?
cards.back: Capture the opening quote and reference that capture where the closing quote is required.
cards.example: (["']).*?\1 finds a simply quoted span; it does not handle escaped quotes robustly.

cards.front: What does (?<name>...) create in JavaScript?
cards.back: A named capturing group.
cards.example: (?<year>[0-9]{4}) captures four digits as year.

cards.front: How do you reference a named group inside a JavaScript pattern?
cards.back: Use \k<name>.
cards.example: (?<letter>[a-z])\k<letter> matches a repeated letter.

cards.front: What does (?=...) mean?
cards.back: A positive lookahead that checks what follows without consuming it.
cards.example: cat(?=s) matches cat in cats.

cards.front: What does (?!...) mean?
cards.back: A negative lookahead that requires the following text not to match its pattern.
cards.example: cat(?!s) matches cat in catnap but not cats.

cards.front: What does (?<=...) mean in a supporting engine?
cards.back: A positive lookbehind that checks preceding text without including it in the match.
cards.example: (?<=USD )[0-9]+ matches 20 in USD 20.

cards.front: What does (?<!...) mean in a supporting engine?
cards.back: A negative lookbehind that requires the preceding text not to match its pattern.
cards.example: (?<![A-Za-z])cat can match cat after a space but not after an ASCII letter.

cards.front: What is a zero-width assertion?
cards.back: A test of a position or surrounding context that consumes no characters itself.
cards.example: A successful ^ assertion does not add a character to the match.

cards.front: Does a lookahead's checked text become part of the full match automatically?
cards.back: No. The assertion checks context without consuming that text.
cards.example: For a(?=b) on ab, the full match is a.

cards.front: What does [\s\S] match in JavaScript?
cards.back: Any character, including line terminators, because every character is either whitespace or nonwhitespace.
cards.example: [\s\S]* can span multiple lines.

cards.front: What does [^0-9]+ match?
cards.back: One or more consecutive characters other than ASCII digits.
cards.example: It finds abc in 12abc34.

cards.front: What does [aeiou] match without i?
cards.back: One lowercase ASCII vowel from the listed set.
cards.example: It finds e in desk.

cards.front: What does [^aeiou] match without i?
cards.back: Any one character not among those lowercase vowels, including consonants, digits, spaces, or punctuation.
cards.example: It matches 7 as well as b.

cards.front: What does [0-9A-Fa-f] match?
cards.back: One hexadecimal digit in ASCII notation.
cards.example: It matches F, a, or 9.

cards.front: What does [ab]+ mean?
cards.back: One or more characters, each independently either a or b. It does not require the repeated pair ab.
cards.example: It matches bbaa.

cards.front: What does \p{L} mean with JavaScript u?
cards.back: A Unicode character in the Letter general category.
cards.example: /\p{L}+/u can match letters in café.

cards.front: What does the negated property escape \P{L} mean with JavaScript u?
cards.back: A character not in the Unicode Letter general category.
cards.example: /\P{L}/u matches the digit in café2.

cards.front: What does \p{Script=Greek} mean with JavaScript u?
cards.back: A character whose Unicode Script property is Greek.
cards.example: /\p{Script=Greek}+/u matches Greek letters such as αβ.

cards.front: How can regex source match a literal plus sign?
cards.back: Escape it as \+ or put it in a suitable character class such as [+].
cards.example: a\+b matches a+b.

cards.front: How can regex source match a literal question mark?
cards.back: Escape it as \? or use [?].
cards.example: why\? matches why?.

cards.front: How can regex source match a literal opening parenthesis?
cards.back: Use \( or an appropriate character class.
cards.example: \(yes\) matches (yes).

cards.front: Why does a string-built regex often need doubled backslashes?
cards.back: The host language processes the string before the regex parser sees it.
cards.example: In JavaScript, new RegExp("\\d+") passes \d+ to the regex parser.

cards.front: How does a regex search differ from whole-input validation?
cards.back: A search may succeed on a substring; validation must explicitly require the entire intended input to conform.
cards.example: [0-9]+ finds digits inside abc12xyz; ^[0-9]+$ rejects that full string in JavaScript without m.

cards.front: What does ^[0-9]{4}$ test in JavaScript without flags?
cards.back: That the whole input consists of exactly four ASCII digits. It does not establish that they represent a sensible year.
cards.example: 2026 passes; 26 does not.

cards.front: What does ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$ test in JavaScript without flags?
cards.back: A simple ASCII identifier beginning with a letter or underscore, followed by letters, digits, or underscores. It does not check reserved words.
cards.example: user_2 passes; 2user fails.

cards.front: What does ^[+-]?[0-9]+$ test in JavaScript without flags?
cards.back: A whole-input ASCII integer representation with an optional sign; it does not check numeric range.
cards.example: -42 and +7 pass.

cards.front: What does ^[0-9]+(?:\.[0-9]+)?$ test in JavaScript without flags?
cards.back: An unsigned decimal form with an integer part and an optional fractional part containing at least one digit.
cards.example: 12.5 passes; .5 and 12. do not.

cards.back: Only the shape of a date-like string, not calendar validity.
cards.example: 2026-99-99 has the required shape but is not a real date.

cards.front: Why is a simple email regex not full email validation?
cards.back: Address syntax and delivery rules are more complex than most short patterns; successful delivery requires checks beyond a regex.
cards.example: A pattern finding one @ does not prove a mailbox exists.

cards.front: What is backtracking in a regex engine?
cards.back: Revisiting earlier matching choices when a later part of the pattern fails.
cards.example: a.*b may give characters back to allow the final b to match.

cards.front: What is catastrophic backtracking?
cards.back: Extremely large amounts of retrying caused by ambiguous patterns on some inputs in backtracking engines.
cards.example: Nested repetition such as (a+)+ followed by a failing condition can be costly.

cards.front: Why should regex matching of untrusted input consider resource limits?
cards.back: Certain patterns or engines can consume excessive time or memory on crafted input.
cards.example: Length limits and a suitable engine can reduce denial-of-service risk.

cards.front: What can go wrong when concatenating unescaped user text into a regex?
cards.back: Regex metacharacters in the text can change the pattern's meaning.
cards.example: User text a.b matches more than the literal a.b if inserted unescaped.

cards.front: Why must regex examples name the engine or flavor?
cards.back: Syntax and semantics differ across JavaScript, Python, PCRE, POSIX, and other engines.
cards.example: \d can mean different digit sets across engines.

cards.front: What should you test besides successful regex matches?
cards.back: Nonmatches, boundaries, empty input, line endings, Unicode cases, and potentially expensive inputs.
cards.example: A date-shape pattern should be tested on extra trailing text as well as a valid-looking date.
